title: Hidden Lakes a Mile Under the Red Sea Are Full of Life
summary:
More than a mile beneath the Red Sea, scientists found something amazing: lakes. Not ordinary lakes, though. These underwater lakes are filled with water so salty that no fish could survive in them, yet tiny microbes thrive there.

The lakes are called brine pools. Researchers from the University of Miami's Rosenstiel School of Marine and Atmospheric Science found them in the Gulf of Aqaba, a northern arm of the Red Sea. They spotted the pools at a depth of 1,770 meters, using a remotely operated underwater vehicle sent down from the research vessel OceanXplorer. The discovery came in the last five minutes of a ten-hour dive. We were very lucky, said Sam Purkis, the professor who led the work.

Brine pools are among the harshest places on Earth. Their water holds extremely high amounts of salt, has unusual chemistry, and contains no oxygen at all. Still, microbes live there in large numbers. Scientists think studying these tough little life forms can help them learn the limits of life on Earth, and that knowledge could guide the search for life on other planets. Earlier research on microbes from Red Sea brine pools has even found molecules with possible anticancer properties.

The pools are also like history books. Because their salty, oxygen-free water preserves evidence so well, they hold traces of tsunamis, flash floods, and earthquakes that happened in the Gulf of Aqaba thousands of years ago. In 2022, Purkis and his colleagues found signs of a 500-year-old underwater landslide that probably caused a large tsunami. Learning more about the region's past could help with planning for coastal areas in Egypt and Saudi Arabia. The study was published in the journal Communications Earth and Environment.
why_it_matters: The microbes in brine pools may hold clues for fighting disease and for finding life beyond Earth, and the pools' record of past tsunamis could help protect coastal communities in Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

background_read: Brine pools are lakes of very salty water that sit on the sea floor, far below the surface.
They form where salty water seeps out of the sea floor and gathers in low spots, too heavy to mix with the lighter sea water above it.
Because the water is so salty and has no oxygen, almost nothing can live there except tiny microbes that have adapted to the harsh conditions.
Scientists explore such places with robot submarines to learn how life can survive in extreme places and what the deep sea can tell us about the past.
